title: MAS-Orchestra: Understanding and Improving Multi-Agent Reasoning Through Holistic Orchestration and Controlled Benchmarks
one_liner: Design the whole multi-agent system at once so the orchestrator can reason about the overall structure instead of composing agents one step at a time.
lead: Many multi-agent systems are assembled sequentially in code: add one subagent, connect one tool, run another step, and hope the overall arrangement makes sense. That process makes it hard to reason about the system as a whole because each local change can alter later coordination, and it also makes it hard to tell when a multi-agent setup truly helps over a single strong agent because the design keeps changing during assembly. MAS-Orchestra trains an orchestrator to generate the full system layout in one shot, and MASBENCH studies when that extra structure is actually useful.

problem.h2: Why hand-built multi-agent setups are hard to trust
paras: A multi-agent system can divide work across planners, searchers, verifiers, and specialists. But building that system step by step creates two problems. First, the designer makes local choices without always seeing the global effect on cost, coordination, and failure handling. Second, even if the system works on a benchmark, it is often unclear whether the extra agents are helping because the task truly benefits from decomposition or merely because the baseline was weak.

This means the field needs both a better orchestration method and a better way to characterize tasks. MAS-Orchestra addresses the first need by letting the orchestrator reason over the entire system design at once. MASBENCH addresses the second by labeling tasks along axes such as depth, horizon, breadth, parallel work, and resistance to disturbance.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Train an orchestrator to choose the whole multi-agent layout in one action space, then study task structure carefully to learn when that layout is worth using.

object.object: The action space for building a multi-agent system

hidden.h2: Task structure fit: the hidden quantity
hidden.name: How well a task matches a multi-agent design
paras: The key quantity is fit between task structure and system structure. Some tasks need long chains of dependent steps, some benefit from several lines of work in parallel, and some can be solved by a single strong agent with no extra coordination cost.

MASBENCH makes this quantity visible by describing tasks along five axes. Once those axes are known, the analysis can ask whether a multi-agent layout is helping because the task truly has decomposable structure or whether the extra agents are unnecessary overhead.

heat.caption: High values mark task properties that often make orchestration choices matter.

reads.html: The hidden quantity is whether this task really benefits from being split across several cooperating units.
MASBENCH characterizes tasks along five structural axes so the study can connect multi-agent gains to task demands instead of treating those gains as universal.

paras: Whole-system orchestration works because system-level design decisions interact with each other. The value of adding a verifier depends on what the solver does, the value of parallel workers depends on the task breadth, and the best stop rule depends on the horizon of the task. Choosing the full structure at once lets the training signal evaluate those interactions directly.

The benchmark analysis works because it prevents vague conclusions. Instead of saying that multi-agent systems are simply better or worse, the paper asks which task properties create room for improvement. That is why the study can show large gains on some tasks while also showing that the gains do not hold everywhere.

A system design and an explanation of when it helps because the task structure justifies the added coordination

math.words: Choose the system layout that maximizes task score minus coordination cost, conditioned on the task's structural properties such as depth, horizon, breadth, and parallel work requirements.
math.equation: best_layout = argmax_layout [ task_score(layout, task) - lambda * coordination_cost(layout) ]
symbols: how well a given layout solves the task
extra cost from communication, routing, and repeated work across units
the full set of roles, calls, and control structure in the system
the problem instance, characterized by axes such as depth and parallel work

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Layout A uses one strong agent. Task score = 78. Coordination cost = 0.
Layout B uses planner + two searchers + verifier. Task score = 90. Coordination cost = 8.
Let lambda = 1. Then objective_A = 78 and objective_B = 90 - 8 = 82.
For a shallow task, suppose Layout B still scores 79 while cost stays 8.
Then objective_B = 79 - 8 = 71, so the single-agent layout is better.
The right layout depends on task structure, not on a fixed preference for more agents.

math.note: The paper uses reinforcement learning over orchestration decisions, but this simplified objective captures the main tradeoff: gains from decomposition must exceed coordination cost.

charts.title: Tasks with useful decomposition
charts.note: Multi-agent layouts help on deeper or broader tasks because several specialized units can divide the work and check one another.

charts.title: Tasks with little structural need
charts.note: Extra agents are not universally useful because communication and repeated work can outweigh any benefit.

items.b: Abstracting subagents can hide important details.
items.html: Treating a subagent as a callable unit helps orchestration because it simplifies system design, but it can conceal internal failure modes that matter for the overall system.

items.b: Benchmark axes may miss task properties.
items.html: Five axes provide structure, but a real application may depend on other factors such as tool reliability or strict timing limits.

items.b: Training can overfit to favored layouts.
items.html: If the training mix over-rewards certain structures, the orchestrator may reuse them too often because it learned a shortcut rather than a general design rule.
Evaluate orchestration against task structure, compare against strong single-agent baselines, and charge explicitly for coordination cost so that only useful layouts survive.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a toy system with a planner, a search unit, and a verifier. Define two task groups: one shallow group that a single agent can solve directly, and one deeper group that benefits from decomposition and checking. Let a simple orchestrator choose either a single-agent layout or a multi-agent layout, then compare task score and runtime.

The demo should prove that whole-system orchestration matters because the best layout depends on task structure, and that multi-agent gains should be credited only when they exceed the cost of coordination.
demo.closing: A useful demo does not argue that more agents are always better. It shows which tasks actually justify them by producing gains that exceed the added coordination cost.
